description.narrative: The Integrated Transport Corridors Project (the Project) is proposed in a context where Guyana continues to be one of the world's fastest growing economies. The country is endowed with extensive grasslands, tropical rainforests, deposits of gold, bauxite, diamonds, abundant water resources, and Oil and Gas (O&G) reserves off its Atlantic coast, which began production in 2019. Guyana's recent economic boom has been driven by the development of its O&G, that brought its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita from US$6,477 in 2019 to over US$18,199 in 2022. Although O&G represents an opportunity for Guyana's development, other similar experiences have shown that it can lead to the neglect of other economic sectors (so-called Dutch Disease). The government is aware of this risk and has implemented measures aimed at mitigating these potential negative impacts. Moreover, spatial disparities in income and multi-dimensional poverty remain, despite improvements in overall poverty rates (reduced from 60.9 percent in 2006 to 48.4 percent in 2019).Guyana's vulnerabilities to natural hazards and climate change pose a critical threat to the sustainability of the country's infrastructure, which the Project is aiming to address. Guyana, considered by the United Nations (UN) as a Small Island Developing State (SIDS), has 90 percent of its population living along the narrow 459-kilometer-long coastal plain, which accounts for only 10 percent of Guyana's land area. As a result, 100 percent of the country's coastal agriculture and 66.4 percent of coastal urban areas are exposed to rising sea levels, coastal flooding, and coastal erosion, with potential GDP losses exceeding 46.4 percent. The limited number of all-weather and resilient roads connecting coastal communities, agricultural areas and tourism destinations, poses a challenge to the formulated vision for regional development and the intended growth of non-oil, tradeable sectors. In response, the Government of Guyana (GoG) and the World Bank Group (WBG) recognize, through Guyana's Country Partnership Framework (CPF) and Guyana's Low Carbon Development Strategy 2030 (LCDS), the urgent need for improved transport infrastructure that is climate resilient, safe and capable of fostering the country's sustainable development. The Project aims to improve the reliability of connectivity to social services, agriculture and tourism destinations by investing in climate resiliency and safety of road interventions in selected areas of the country, thereby supporting the diversification of the economy. In addition, the Project will strengthen the overall road sector management for strategic prioritization of investments in the transport sector, with climate, human development and competitiveness at its core.The GoG has requested the World Bank's support for improving climate resilience and safety along strategic road corridors. The request for road upgrades to be financed by the World Bank is recognized as a regional priority given the joint declaration by the Presidents of the Co-operative Republic of Guyana, the Federative Republic of Brazil and the Republic of Suriname at the 46th Regular Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government of CARICOM in February 2024. The Project will finance the upgrade of identified road corridors/sections in selected regions of Guyana, with a focus on the coastal regions, also strengthening the GoG's institutional capacity in the road transport sector with considerations of climate change, road safety, citizen engagement and gender.The Project aims to build climate resilience in transport infrastructure to support coastal and inland connectivity, regional integration, expansion of the agricultural and tourism sectors, and safety for all road users. This will be done through four components, described below.Component 1: Climate resilient and safe road corridors improvement (US$144 million). This component will improve (rehabilitate and upgrade) road corridors in selected areas of Regions 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 of Guyana, with an initial list of potential strategic roads identified by GoG for investments reflected in Table 1 of the PAD, to be further assessed for financing under the Project based on a 2-step screening framework. The Project will aim to reduce climate risks and bring additional benefits such as promoting inclusive job creation, improving access to social services, and enhancing economic opportunities. Activities under this component include design studies, civil works and supervision of selected regional road corridors, with maintenance to be considered for a specific pilot road. The studies and works will incorporate: (i) climate resilient interventions (e.g. improvement of drainage systems, slope stabilization, among others, with more details in the next paragraph); (ii) select road safety interventions based on a road safety inspection of the existing road, respectively road safety audit for each of the four stages financed under this component (e.g. crash barriers, road signs and markings, raised pedestrian crossings, traffic calming measures, and others); (iii) active mobility infrastructure with gender considerations (e.g. dedicated pedestrian pathways/sidewalks and 2- and 3-wheelers lanes for Non-Motorized Transportation - NMT), together with safe bus stops, encouraging a shift towards active transport mobility from car-dependency while providing a safe space to address women's security, and informed by communitarian mobility plans undertaken under the Project; and (iv) Information and Communications Technology solutions for weight-in motion systems and automated traffic enforcement (e.g. speed management). The civil works will include roads, bridges, and culverts. Additionally, Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) will be prioritized to address climate resilience.To respond to the climate change threats, this component has climate adaptation as a core objective in its design and contributes to climate mitigation. The road corridors under this component will be selected based on their climate vulnerability and exposure to climate change. To that end, approximately 85 percent of Component 1 would finance climate change adaptation of most vulnerable roads to guarantee that transport connectivity is sustained in a country highly exposed to climate change vulnerabilities. The climate resilient interventions, activity (i) described above, will reduce the physical climate risk and build the adaptive capacity of selected roads through dedicated measures to ensure resilience to the expected impacts of climate change and its evolving patterns. Activities (ii) – (iv) are complementary to the climate resilient interventions and will focus on mitigating road safety or Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emission risks. The climate resilience measures include: (i) sealing of gravel roads, which will increase resistance to intense water runoffs, in turn preventing surface and platform erosion; (ii) protecting slopes against landslides and embankment erosion (due to heavy rainfall) through bioengineering (NBS) and civil works (gabions, retaining walls, ripraps, etc.); (iii) raising embankments above high water levels to protect the road structure against erosion, so that roads are passable year round, including during rainy seasons, and to minimize disruption; and (iv) constructing culverts adapted to future climate events.Component 2: Institutional strengthening for road sector management (US$7 million)a. Sub-Component 2.1: Road safety (US$3 million). This sub-component will finance activities in line with the Safe System approach, addressing: (i) road safety management; (ii) safety assessments of the main road network through climate vulnerability lenses; (iii) mobility studies for enabling NMT; and (iv) pilot interventions in high-risk locations in selected areas. Activity (i) will include the selection and financing of priority actions under the Road Safety Action Plan for Guyana for 2024-
To improve climate resilient and safe road connectivity in selected regions of Guyana and, in case of an Eligible Crisis or Emergency, respond promptly and effectively to it.
